traveler: Harriet Tubman (born Araminta "Minty" Ross; Harriet Tubman Davis)
title: The Marsh to the Brick House: Minty Ross, the Conductor, and the Combahee
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Neck, the Marsh, and the Weight

stops.name: Peter's Neck, the birth without a record
stops.date_confidence: disputed on both counts. No birth record survives; competing documents support 1815, 1820, 1822, and 1825. Popular accounts long placed the birth at the Brodess farm at Bucktown, while Kate Clifford Larson's genealogical reconstruction places it on Anthony Thompson's land at Peter's Neck, where Rit was then working. The pin follows the Peter's Neck reconstruction and is approximate to the Blackwater district.
stops.campa: A daughter is born to Harriet Green, called Rit, and to Ben Ross, on ground Rit is working in the southern neck of the county. They name her Araminta and call her Minty. Nobody writes down the day. Maryland counts her the property of Edward Brodess and counts enslavement as inherited through the mother, so the title that owns her runs through the woman who bore her. The country she is born into is tidal creek, loblolly pine, black mud, and muskrat. It floods and drains twice a day. Rit's older children are Brodess property under the same rule.
suggested_refs: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park, Church Creek, Maryland, which preserves the Blackwater landscape of the birth and the escape network
sources: Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)

stops.name: The Brodess farm at Bucktown, hired out at five
stops.date_confidence: approximate. NPS and Wikipedia give her age at the first hiring as about five or six, which places it around 1827-28; no document fixes the year.
stops.campa: Edward Brodess hires the child out for cash. She is five or six years old, sent among strangers as a nursemaid and a house servant, returned when she sickens or gives trouble, then sent out again. Later the work gets heavier: traplines in winter water, then the field, then timber. Each posting puts her on ground she has not seen before, and she is expected to find her own way to it and back, which is how she comes to know whose land runs where and which roads carry patrols. The wage is paid to Brodess.
suggested_refs: The Brodess farm site at Bucktown, Dorchester County
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Bucktown Village Store, the weight
stops.date_confidence: approximate. Accounts date the injury to about 1835 and give her age as twelve or thirteen. A 2023 medical-history reassessment (Balmuth and Scammell, PMC10713879) reads the lifelong seizures, hypersomnia episodes, and visionary states as sequelae of traumatic brain injury.
stops.campa: She is twelve or thirteen, sent to the store at Bucktown on an errand, and an overseer is there after an enslaved man who has left his work without leave. The man breaks for the door. The overseer throws a two-pound weight across the room; the man is not hit, and the girl is. The iron opens her skull. She is carried back bleeding, laid on a loom bench, and put into the field again before the wound has closed. For the rest of her life she falls asleep without warning, mid-sentence, mid-step, and wakes speaking of what she has just been shown.
suggested_refs: The Bucktown Village Store, 4303 Bucktown Road, Cambridge, Maryland, still standing
sources: Balmuth and Scammell, medical-history reassessment, PMC10713879 (2023)

stops.name: Stewart's Canal, timber and tidewater with Ben Ross
stops.date_confidence: decade only. NPS places the timber work in the late 1830s and 1840s without fixing years; the canal coordinate is approximate to the cut running from Parsons Creek toward the Blackwater near Madison.
stops.campa: John Stewart hires Ben Ross to run his timbering, and Ross brings his daughter into the work. She drives oxen, cuts, hauls, and helps raft logs down a canal that enslaved and free Black crews dug by hand from Parsons Creek toward the Blackwater, where the timber goes out by boat for Baltimore. Her father knows the woods, the tides, and the men who move on them, free Black watermen and sailors carrying news up and down the bay. The rafts move when the water moves; the crews stand on the bank and wait when it does not.
suggested_refs: Stewart's Canal, dug by hand between Parsons Creek and the Blackwater River, within the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park

stops.name: Dorchester County, the marriage that changes nothing
stops.date_confidence: approximate. NPS gives the marriage as around 1844. The change of name from Araminta to Harriet is traditionally dated to this period but is not fixed by any document.
stops.campa: She marries John Tubman, a free Black man of the county, and takes his name; by now she has also put down Araminta and taken her mother's, so that Minty Ross becomes Harriet Tubman. The marriage alters nothing that matters. Maryland holds that a child follows the condition of the mother, and that a wife brings her condition in with her, so she remains Edward Brodess's property inside a free man's house, and any child of the marriage would be born Brodess's too. She stays in that arrangement five years.
suggested_refs: Maryland's partus sequitur ventrem statute, under which her marriage to a free man left her status untouched

stops.name: Bucktown, Edward Brodess dies in debt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The account of her praying first for his conversion and then for his death comes from Bradford's authorized biography, which is Tubman's own telling at one remove and was produced to raise money.
stops.campa: Edward Brodess dies in March with his estate in debt, and an indebted estate in Maryland is settled the way Maryland settles debts: by selling people. Two of Rit's daughters have already gone south in a chain gang and are not heard from again. Tubman has spent the winter praying that Brodess be changed in his heart, and then, when he keeps bringing buyers to look at her, praying that he be taken out of the world. He is taken out of the world. She says afterward that she would have given herself to get the prayer back.
stops.quote: An' so, I prayed all night long for master, till the first of March; an' all the time he was bringing people to look at me, an' trying to sell me. Den we heard dat some of us was gwine to be sole to go wid de chain-gang down to de cotton an' rice fields.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The Brodess estate inventory and debt proceedings, Dorchester County, 1849
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Poplar Neck, the first attempt and the turning back
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date is fixed by the runaway advertisement Eliza Brodess placed three weeks later, which names the three of them and the day.
stops.campa: With her brothers Ben and Henry she leaves on the seventeenth of September, moving north through Caroline County toward the Choptank and the ground at Poplar Neck where their father is hired out. Somewhere on that road the brothers change their minds. What they are walking away from is certain and what they are walking toward is a rumor, and they want to go back. They insist she come with them, and she goes, because two turning and one going is a party that gets everybody caught. Within the month she leaves again, alone.
suggested_refs: Poplar Neck, Caroline County, where Ben Ross was hired and which served repeatedly as a staging ground
sources: Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)

stops.name: Cambridge, one hundred dollars each
stops.date_confidence: attested. The advertisement in the Cambridge Democrat of 3 October 1849 survives and is the only contemporary price ever set on her.
stops.campa: Eliza Brodess pays for a notice in the Cambridge Democrat naming three runaways from the estate: Minty, Ben, and Harry. One hundred dollars for each of them if they are taken outside Maryland, less if taken within it. Three hundred dollars is what the estate reckons the three are worth to get back. A later century will raise the figure to forty thousand and add the words dead or alive, and will do it in her honor, as though the real number were too small to carry her. The newspaper survives and says one hundred dollars.
suggested_refs: Cambridge Democrat, 3 October 1849, runaway advertisement for Minty, Ben, and Harry
sources: Cambridge Democrat, 3 October 1849, as reproduced and discussed in NPS materials
Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)

stops.name: Philadelphia, the line
stops.date_confidence: month approximate. NPS places the successful escape in the autumn of 1849; the route through Delaware and the day of arrival are not documented, and the Quaker and free Black waypoints along it come from later route reconstruction rather than from any contemporary record.
stops.campa: She comes in alone, by night travel and by the help of people whose names the record mostly does not keep, up through Delaware and across the Pennsylvania line into a city where the law cannot yet reach back for her. She is about twenty-seven. She finds work as a domestic and a cook, hotel kitchens and private houses, and she keeps her own wages for the first time in her life. Around her is the largest free Black community in the country, and a Vigilance Committee that has been moving people north for twenty years out of an office on North Fifth Street.
stops.quote: When I found I had crossed dat _line_, I looked at my hands to see if I was de same pusson. There was such a glory ober ebery ting; de sun came like gold through the trees, and ober the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaben.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society office and Vigilance Committee, 107 N. Fifth Street, Philadelphia
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Philadelphia, a stranger in a strange land
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The resolve is undated; it is placed here because the first rescue follows within a year. The wording is Bradford's transcription of Tubman's own retelling twenty years after the fact.
stops.campa: Freedom, once she is standing in it, turns out to be a room with nobody else in it. Her mother, her father, her brothers and sisters, her husband are two hundred miles south and still owned, and a free woman in Philadelphia is a woman who has left them there. She settles the question in the only terms she keeps, as a bargain made directly with God on the understanding that she will do the walking. Nobody at the Vigilance Committee asks her to go back. Within a year she is back.
stops.quote: I would make a home in the North and bring them there, God helping me. Oh, how I prayed then; I said to de Lord, 'I'm gwine to hole stiddy on to _you_, an' I _know_ you'll see me through.'
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: William Still, The Underground Rail Road (1872), the Vigilance Committee's own records of the people she brought in
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Cambridge, Kessiah at the auction block
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The mechanics of the escape during the sale come from William Still and later synthesis rather than from a court record of the auction.
stops.campa: Her niece Kessiah Bowley is put up for sale at Cambridge with her two children. Kessiah's husband John Bowley, a free Black shipwright, stands in the crowd through the bidding, and when the sale breaks he walks his own wife and children out of the building and hides them until dark, then takes them up the Chesapeake in a boat. This is the first rescue Tubman runs, and she is not in Dorchester County for any of it. She spends it in Baltimore, waiting at the other end of the water.
suggested_refs: The Dorchester County Courthouse at Cambridge, where enslaved people of the county were sold
sources: William Still, The Underground Rail Road (1872), referenced via NPS articles

stops.name: Baltimore, the house of Tom Tubman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the exact address of the safe house is not recorded.
stops.campa: The Bowleys come up the bay by boat and are put into a safe house kept by Tom Tubman, her husband's brother, in a city where free and enslaved Black people work the same wharves and the difference between them is a paper in a pocket. She meets them there and takes them on north. From here the pattern holds and does not change for ten years: somebody inside the county gets a family as far as the water or the road, and she takes them from that point on. The two halves of the work are done by different people who mostly never meet.
suggested_refs: The free Black maritime community of Fells Point, Baltimore, and its role in Chesapeake escapes

stops.name: Dorchester County, John Tubman has married again
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the year; the month is inferred from the autumn party that followed. The detail of the suit of clothes bought with her wages is Bradford's.
stops.campa: She comes back for her husband with a suit of clothes bought out of her own wages, and finds that John Tubman has married a woman named Caroline and does not intend to go anywhere. Her first thought is to make a scene at the door and let herself be taken. She thinks better of it, sends word instead through the quarter that she is in the neighborhood and going north, and asks who else wants to come. Eleven people leave with her before the year is out. The suit of clothes is not mentioned again in any account.
suggested_refs: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman, on the return for John Tubman
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), docsouth.unc.edu/neh/bradford

stops.name: St. Catharines, the law follows them into the free states
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the shift; the month of her first Canadian crossing is not fixed. NPS dates her use of St. Catharines from the early 1850s.
stops.campa: The Fugitive Slave Act has made every marshal in every free state an arm of the Maryland courts, and a Black person in Philadelphia or Boston can now be seized on an affidavit and put on a southbound train with no hearing worth the name. The line she crossed in 1849 has moved. She moves with it, running people the whole further length of New York State and over the Niagara frontier into Canada West, where St. Catharines has a growing town of refugees and wage work in the canal trade. Canada does not send them back.
suggested_refs: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 and the northward extension of Underground Railroad routes into Canada West
sources: NPS general synthesis on the Underground Railroad and fugitive slave law

stops.name: Wilmington, Thomas Garrett's shoes
stops.date_confidence: decade rather than date. Garrett's station operated throughout the 1850s and she passed through it many times; no single visit is dated here, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Thomas Garrett keeps a shoe business and an open secret at 227 Shipley Street. He is a Quaker, a federal court has already fined him into bankruptcy for exactly this, and he told that court he intended to go on doing it. She comes to his door many times across the decade with parties of two and of eight and of eleven, and leaves with money, food, and shoes, because on a hundred-mile walk the thing that fails first is footwear. He writes about her parties to his correspondents in England and in Philadelphia.
suggested_refs: Thomas Garrett's correspondence with British and Philadelphia abolitionists describing Tubman's parties

stops.name: Cape May, the wages that pay for the returns
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1852-1854; the specific season is not fixed.
stops.campa: Between missions she cooks. Cape May's resort hotels take on Black staff for the summer season, and she works their kitchens and laundries through several of them, banking what she is paid. This is the half of the operation nobody makes a statue of and the half without which the other half does not happen. Going back into Maryland costs boat fare, food, bribes, and whatever it takes to keep an infant quiet on a night crossing. The money for it comes out of a hotel wage, paid by the week.
suggested_refs: The Cape May resort hotels that employed Black seasonal staff in the 1850s

stops.name: Camden, the Brinkleys and Abraham Gibbs
stops.date_confidence: decade rather than date. The Camden station and its agents are attested for the 1850s; the date orders the segment and no single passage through it is documented.
stops.campa: North of the Maryland line the route runs hand to hand on free Black households and Quaker farms. The Delaware corridor is about a hundred miles of ordinary road, with people standing at intervals along it who have agreed in advance to lie to a constable. Not one of them can afford what he is doing. At Camden the brothers William and Nat Brinkley and Abraham Gibbs keep a station, feeding parties in the dark and moving them out by wagon toward Dover and Wilmington under a load of produce.
suggested_refs: The free Black and Quaker station network of Kent and New Castle Counties, Delaware

stops.name: Jacob Jackson's farm, the letter signed with another man's name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The letter itself does not survive; its wording is preserved in Bradford and in later NPS accounts of the Jackson family.
stops.campa: Her brothers are to be sold after Christmas, and there is no way to warn them that a postmaster will not read first. Jacob Jackson, a free Black farmer and veterinarian in the county, gets mail, and his mail is opened as a matter of course. So the letter she dictates is addressed to him, signed with the name of his adopted son William Henry Jackson, and speaks of the old ship of Zion coming along and of brothers who should be watching and ready to step aboard. The white men who open it can make nothing of it. Jackson, who has no brothers, reads it correctly.
suggested_refs: NPS, 'New Beginnings: Harriet Tubman, Jacob Jackson, and the Eastern Shore'

stops.name: Poplar Neck, Christmas in the fodder house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season. The detail of Ben Ross keeping himself blindfolded so that he could swear he had not seen them comes from Bradford and is repeated by NPS; it is family testimony, not a document of the day.
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve she takes her brothers Robert, Ben, and Henry out of the county, with Ben's fiancee Jane and two other men, and holds them all day in the fodder house at Poplar Neck. Their mother is a few yards off, cooking a Christmas dinner for sons she believes are coming, while the sons lie in the corn listening to her move around the kitchen. Their father brings them food with a cloth tied over his eyes so that he can swear afterward, and swear truthfully, that he has not seen them. Then eighty miles of December road, and no fires.
stops.quote: Dere's _two_ things I've got a _right_ to, and dese are, Death or Liberty--one or tother I mean to have. No one will take me back alive; I shall fight for my liberty, and when de time has come for me to go, de Lord will let dem kill me.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The Ross family fodder house at Poplar Neck, Caroline County, Christmas 1854
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Dover, the Dover Eight betrayed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season. Tubman was not with the Dover Eight; the stop marks the point on her own network where the betrayal broke it open and forced the removal of her parents.
stops.campa: A party of eight out of Dorchester is sold to the sheriff for the reward money by a man they trusted in Dover, and the betrayal runs backward down the line to everyone who had fed them. Her father is named. Ben Ross has been sheltering freedom seekers for years, and both Delaware and Maryland now want the man who did it. Seven years of getting people out of that county have rested on a network she did not build by herself, and the network has just become the exposure. She has weeks, not months.
suggested_refs: The Dover Eight, betrayed in Delaware in March 1857, and the pursuit of Ben Ross that followed
sources: NPS biographical synthesis of the family rescue missions

stops.name: Salem Chapel, St. Catharines, Ben and Rit among the exiles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year. The improvised cart, and the horse bought to draw it, come from Bradford and the family accounts; the month of arrival in Canada is not documented.
stops.campa: She goes down and brings her parents out, an old man and an old woman who cannot walk it. She buys a horse, sets a board across a pair of wheels, drives them to the railroad and north through New York State to the Niagara frontier. Around Salem Chapel on Geneva Street there is by now a settlement of people she carried, several of them her own brothers, worshipping in a British Methodist Episcopal congregation of refugees. Ben and Rit Ross spend that winter in Canada. Neither of them has been north of Delaware before.
suggested_refs: Salem Chapel British Methodist Episcopal Church, 92 Geneva Street, St. Catharines, Ontario

stops.name: St. Catharines, John Brown calls her General
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by NPS. Wikipedia dates Brown's Chatham constitutional convention to 8-10 May 1858, and the two sources are not fully reconciled on the sequence; neither firmly places Tubman inside the Chatham hall, so no stop is made there.
stops.campa: John Brown comes north into Canada West looking for soldiers and finds a woman who has been running a supply line into a slave state for eight years without losing anybody on it. He asks her about routes, about mountains, about which men in which county will hold. He calls her General Tubman and goes on calling her that in front of other people. She helps him recruit among the refugees at St. Catharines while he plans a convention at Chatham to write a constitution for a country that does not exist. She thinks he is right about the war.
stops.quote: Mr. Phillips, I bring you one of the best and bravest persons on this continent--_General_ Tubman, as we call her.
stops.quote_source: John Brown introducing Tubman to Wendell Phillips, as recounted by Phillips and printed in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The First Baptist Church, 135 King Street East, Chatham, Ontario, where Brown's May 1858 convention sat

stops.name: Auburn, seven acres from Frances Seward
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not fixed. NPS gives the purchase as roughly seven acres for $1,200 on favorable terms.
stops.campa: Frances Seward, whose husband is a United States senator, sells her seven acres on the southern edge of Auburn for twelve hundred dollars, on terms a woman with no capital can actually meet. Selling land to a Black woman who is herself legally a fugitive is not a neutral act in 1859, and the Sewards do it anyway, and quietly. Her parents come down from Canada, where they were cold and where nobody had asked them if they wanted to go. Brothers, nieces, boarders, and strangers follow. The house fills and stays full for fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Tubman residence, 182 South Street, Auburn, New York, now part of Harriet Tubman National Historical Park

stops.name: New Bedford, absent when the armory is taken
stops.date_confidence: contradicted and left unresolved. Sources place her at New Bedford and at New York City for the same week, on the same secondary reconstruction, and the reason given for her absence from Harpers Ferry is illness, which no contemporary document confirms. The pin follows the New Bedford reading and does not settle the question.
stops.campa: Brown takes the federal armory at Harpers Ferry on the sixteenth of October with twenty-one men, holds it two days, and is hanged in December. She had helped recruit some of the men who die on the engine-house floor, and she never afterward speaks of him as anything but a martyr. She is not there. One account puts her at New Bedford that week and another at New York City, and the reason offered for her absence is illness, offered by people who were not with her either. Which account is right, and whether she was ill at all, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: John Brown's Fort, the armory engine house at Harpers Ferry, West Virginia

stops.name: Auburn, the last party in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the date of arrival. That this was the final mission is known only in retrospect; nothing at the time marked it as the last.
stops.campa: The last party she brings out of Maryland reaches Auburn at the end of December, members of the Ennalls family among them, an infant carried the whole distance. Martha and David Wright take them in, one node of a chain that now runs from a fodder house on the Choptank to a Quaker parlor in central New York. She has been going back into that country for eleven years and is planning the next trip. South Carolina voted itself out of the Union eight days ago.
suggested_refs: The Martha Coffin Wright household at Auburn, station and correspondence hub of the Underground Railroad in central New York
sources: NPS biographical synthesis of the Underground Railroad missions

stops.name: Port Royal, among the people the planters left
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month of arrival is not fixed. The detail that she supported herself by selling pies and root beer rather than drawing army rations comes from Bradford's account.
stops.campa: She comes south to the Sea Islands, where the planters have run and the people who were their property are living on abandoned cotton land and are called contraband in the federal paperwork. She nurses, cooks, and runs a wash house, and sells pies and root beer at night to pay her own way, refusing army rations because drawing them would set her above the people she came for. Within a year she is drawing on a government fund to pay Lowcountry men who know the rivers, and sending them out to look.
suggested_refs: The Port Royal Experiment in the occupied Sea Islands, 1862-1865
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Beaufort, the ice and the flies
stops.date_confidence: period rather than date. The hospital work runs across her whole time in the Department of the South; the date orders the segment. The account is her own, given to Bradford years afterward.
stops.campa: In the contraband hospital at Beaufort the men are dying of dysentery and of the wounds the surgeons have run out of hands for. She goes in early with a chunk of ice in a basin and a sponge, nobody paying her for any of it, and works down the line of them, one man at a time, driving the flies off a face before she washes it. She uses roots she learned in the Blackwater marshes on a fever the army surgeons cannot break, and keeps on using them after the surgeons stop asking where the medicine comes from. The ice she buys out of the pie money.
stops.quote: Well, Missus, I'd go to de hospital, I would, early eb'ry mornin'. I'd get a big chunk of ice, I would, and put it in a basin, and fill it with water; den I'd take a sponge and begin. Fust man I'd come to, I'd thrash away de flies, an' dey'd rise, dey would, like bees roun' a hive.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The contraband hospital at Beaufort, South Carolina, and Tubman's later pension claim for nursing service
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Beaufort waterfront, the gunboats cast off
stops.date_confidence: attested to the night of 1-2 June 1863.
stops.campa: Three gunboats cast off from the Beaufort waterfront after dark carrying about three hundred soldiers of the Second South Carolina Volunteers, a regiment of formerly enslaved men that exists at all because Abraham Lincoln's proclamation of the first of January made Black enlistment federal policy. Their colonel is James Montgomery, out of Kansas and out of John Brown's war. Tubman has spent months paying scouts to bring back where the torpedoes are sunk in the Combahee and which plantations still have people standing on them. She is aboard.
stops.quote: Mrs. Harriet Tubman, a most remarkable woman, and invaluable as a scout.
stops.quote_source: Colonel James Montgomery, official commendation printed in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The Beaufort waterfront departure point, now Henry C. Chambers Waterfront Park
sources: Edda L. Fields-Black, Combee (Oxford University Press, 2024)

stops.name: Combahee Ferry, seven hundred and fifty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested. The count varies by source: contemporary press and older accounts give more than 700, while Edda L. Fields-Black's archival reconstruction gives 756. More than 150 of the men liberated enlisted in Union service.
stops.campa: The boats go up the river past the mines because she knows where the mines are. Troops land at the plantations and fire the rice mills, the whistle sounds, and the fields empty toward the water: people running with children on their hips and pails of smoking rice still on their heads, and the drivers behind them cannot turn a single one back. The rowboats fill and swamp. By morning the gunboats have carried more than seven hundred and fifty people down to Beaufort, and within weeks over a hundred and fifty of the men are in uniform.
stops.quote: We laughed, an' laughed, an' laughed. Here you'd see a woman wid a pail on her head, rice a smokin' in it jus as she'd taken it from de fire.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The Combahee Ferry crossing, now the Harriet Tubman Bridge on US 17
Edda L. Fields-Black, Combee (2024), which reconstructs the raid from the pension files of the people freed
sources: Edda L. Fields-Black, Combee (Oxford University Press, 2024)

stops.name: Auburn, the book written to pay her debts
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the project; the book circulates from late 1868 with an 1869 date on the title page. Bradford's text is a fundraising work assembled at speed from interviews and testimonials, not a memoir, and Tubman was not conventionally literate.
stops.campa: She is past fifty, land-poor, feeding a household of dependents on nothing, and the government that used her for three years has paid her almost none of it. Her Auburn neighbors set the writer Sarah Bradford to make a book out of her, and Bradford does it fast, in a hurry to sail for Europe, stitching interviews and letters into a pamphlet with an 1869 date on the title page. It is sold to clear her debts. Every account of her early life written since, including the careful ones, runs back through it.
stops.quote: I haint got no heart to go and see the sufferings of my people played on de stage. I've heard 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' read, and I tell you Mrs. Stowe's pen hasn't begun to paint what slavery is as I have seen it at the far South. I've seen de _real ting_, and I don't want to see it on no stage or in no teater.
stops.quote_source: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), and its 1886 rewriting as Harriet, the Moses of Her People
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Auburn, the letter that comes from Rochester
stops.date_confidence: attested. The letter in Bradford is datelined Rochester, 29 August 1868. Douglass wrote it at his own house and never came to Auburn for it; it reaches her as a document for the book.
stops.campa: Bradford wants endorsements, and what comes back is from the men who ran the public half of the war she fought in the dark: Gerrit Smith, Wendell Phillips, and from Rochester, on the twenty-ninth of August, Frederick Douglass. Douglass has been photographed, published, and applauded on two continents. He writes that he has wrought in the day and she in the night, that his witnesses were crowds and hers were a few trembling and foot-sore people in the woods, and that except for John Brown he knows nobody who has willingly taken more.
stops.quote: I have wrought in the day--you in the night. I have had the applause of the crowd and the satisfaction that comes of being approved by the multitude, while the most that you have done has been witnessed by a few trembling, scared, and foot-sore bondmen and women.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Douglass, letter to Harriet Tubman, Rochester, 29 August 1868, printed in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821
suggested_refs: The testimonial letters of Frederick Douglass, Gerrit Smith, and Wendell Phillips printed at the front of Bradford's 1869 edition
sources: Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869), Project Gutenberg #57821

stops.name: Auburn, marrying Nelson Davis
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Auburn marriage record. The adoption of the infant Gertie around 1874 is [R]: it rests on family photographs and Auburn household tradition rather than on a document reached in this pass.
stops.campa: She marries Nelson Davis in Auburn before a crowded church. He is a bricklayer, formerly enslaved in North Carolina, a veteran of the Eighth United States Colored Troops, and something over twenty years younger than his wife, whose own age nobody including herself can state exactly. He has tuberculosis in him already and will not outlive her. A few years on they take in an infant girl and name her Gertie. No adoption paper for her has been found; the family photographs and the neighbors are the whole of the record.
suggested_refs: The service record and pension file of Private Nelson Davis, 8th United States Colored Troops

stops.name: Auburn, the gold that was not there
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Auburn press coverage; the month is not fixed.
stops.campa: Two men come to Auburn with a story about a trunk of Southern gold, a fortune in it, hers for two thousand dollars in cash. She raises the money on the strength of the South Street property, which is the only thing she owns outright. She goes out with them at night to see the trunk. She is chloroformed, tied, and left in the woods, and the money is gone before morning. The Auburn papers print all of it, her name and the amount included. She needs the two thousand dollars.
suggested_refs: Auburn press coverage of the 1873 gold swindle
sources: Auburn Citizen coverage as referenced via auburnpub.com retrospective

stops.name: The Capitol, two thousand dollars refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not fixed. The sum is corrected here: the bill sought $2,000, not the $5,000 that circulates in secondary accounts. A committee recommended a smaller figure and nothing was enacted.
stops.campa: Clinton MacDougall of New York and Gerry Hazelton of Wisconsin bring in a bill to pay her two thousand dollars for her wartime service. She has receipts, and written commendations from officers she served under. The claim is awkward for the government in a way that has nothing to do with whether the service occurred: she was a scout and a spy, and the army does not commission Black women as scouts and spies, so there is no rank for back pay to attach to. A committee recommends less. Nothing passes.
suggested_refs: National Archives, 'The Claim of Harriet Tubman,' archives.gov/legislative/features/claim-of-harriet-tubman
sources: history.house.gov, House History Blog on Tubman legislative history

stops.name: Auburn, the fire and the brick house
stops.date_confidence: month only. NPS says a careless boarder set the wood-frame house on fire in 1880; Wikipedia narrows it to February. No source reached supports the specific day of 10 February that circulates. The brick replacement was built in 1881-1882.
stops.campa: A boarder is careless with a fire and the wooden farmhouse she bought from Frances Seward burns down. She has been taking in the old, the sick, and the destitute there for twenty years without asking anyone what they had done, which is how the boarder came to be under the roof to begin with. The family rebuilds in brick over the next two years, Nelson Davis's trade and the labor of Black neighbors. Whatever papers she had kept were in the wooden one.
suggested_refs: The brick Tubman residence at 182 South Street, built 1881-1882 on the site of the burned farmhouse

stops.name: Auburn, the widow of Private Davis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is not fixed in the sources reached. Tuberculosis is the cause commonly cited and appears in the pension file record.
stops.campa: Nelson Davis dies after nineteen years of marriage, of the tuberculosis he brought home from the army. His widow is left with the house, the people living in it, and a mortgage. The war she served in her own body has yielded her nothing she can file: there is no muster roll anywhere with her name written against a rank. The war he served in has left a service record, a regiment, and a number. She files as the relict of Private Nelson Davis of the Eighth United States Colored Troops.
suggested_refs: The Nelson Davis pension file, National Archives
sources: NPS synthesis of Tubman's late life

stops.name: Washington, the National Association of Colored Women
stops.date_confidence: the Washington convention of July 1896 is attested, though sources vary on whether to call her a founding member or a participant, and the more conservative reading is used. The quotation is separately dated to 1896 by the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth suffrage exhibit, which does not fix the city; Rochester and Boston are both offered. The two are not the same occasion and are set together here only because the record dates both to that year.
stops.campa: She sits with the Black clubwomen founding a national federation in Washington, an old woman among organizers thirty and forty years younger who get to their feet when she comes into the room. She has been on the suffrage circuit for years now, sharing platforms with white women who present her as evidence and Black women who claim her as ancestry. Asked what entitles her to speak on the question, she answers that she never ran her train off the track and never lost a passenger.
stops.quote: never ran my train off the track and never lost a passenger
stops.quote_source: Tubman, addressing a suffrage convention in 1896, as given in the Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth suffrage exhibit; the exhibit does not fix the city
suggested_refs: The founding convention of the National Association of Colored Women, Washington, July 1896
sources: NPS synthesis of Tubman's suffrage and club-movement activity

stops.name: The Capitol, H.R. 4982
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of introduction. The bill number and the outcome are confirmed by the National Archives; the reduction and rerouting through widow and nurse categories is documented in the congressional record.
stops.campa: Sereno Payne introduces H.R. 4982, asking twenty-five dollars a month for her own service: three years of nursing, scouting, and spying in the Department of the South. The House is willing. The Senate is not willing at that figure and is not willing on that theory. To pay her as a scout would put in the statute book a sentence saying the United States Army had employed a Black woman as a scout. The Senate rewrites the bill into the two categories the government keeps for women, widow and nurse, at a lower rate.
suggested_refs: National Archives, 'The Claim of Harriet Tubman'

stops.name: Massachusetts General Hospital, the surgery without ether
stops.date_confidence: late 1890s only. No source reached fixes the year; the specific 1898 that circulates is unsupported and the date here orders the segment. The surgery itself is accepted in the biographical literature. The refusal of anesthesia and the bullet between her teeth survive only in Tubman's own retrospective telling, not in any hospital record.
stops.campa: The wound from the Bucktown store has been in her head sixty years and the pain has got past bearing. Surgeons at Massachusetts General open her skull to relieve it. She tells it afterward as a soldier's story: that she declined the ether, that she bit down on a bullet the way she had watched men do it in the field hospitals at Beaufort, and that she lay there through the whole of it. There is no hospital record of the bullet. There is her account, given the same way each time, to people who wrote it down.
suggested_refs: Balmuth and Scammell, the 2023 medical-history reassessment of Tubman's head injury and its lifelong sequelae

stops.name: Auburn, a scout, nurse, cook and spy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not fixed. The affidavit is held in the congressional claim file at the National Archives.
stops.campa: She swears an affidavit describing what she did in the war in six words: a scout, nurse, cook and spy. It is a summary of three years and it is also a legal instrument, filed to make a bureaucracy write down a sentence that no muster roll in the United States contains. She is somewhere past seventy. Neighbors help her gather the letters Union officers wrote about her at the time, in their own hands, and those go into the file behind the affidavit.
suggested_refs: The Harriet Tubman claim file, Records of the U.S. House of Representatives, National Archives

stops.name: The White House, twenty dollars a month
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The National Archives page prints 19 January 1899 as the date on the bill document, not the date of enactment, and says only that Congress passed and the President signed H.R. 4982 in 1899. Wikipedia dates the approval of the $20 pension to February 1899, and that is the date used here.
stops.campa: Congress passes and William McKinley signs the act raising her pension to twenty dollars a month, and it is granted on her husband's service, not on hers. She has been drawing eight dollars a month as Nelson Davis's widow since 1895, along with a five hundred dollar lump sum. At the end of a fifty-year argument the government has paid her, correctly and in full, as a soldier's wife. It never at any point pays her as what she was. The affidavit saying what she was stays in the file.
suggested_refs: H.R. 4982, A bill granting a pension to Harriet Tubman Davis, National Archives

stops.name: Auburn, the Home opens under her name
stops.date_confidence: attested. Incorporated 3 December 1895, the adjoining twenty-five acres bought in 1896, the property deeded to the AME Zion Church in 1903, the Home formally opened 23 June 1908.
stops.campa: In 1896 she buys twenty-five acres next to her own land at auction, bidding against her neighbors with no money in her pocket, and incorporates on it a home for aged and indigent Black people. Running it beats her. There are mortgages, and there is an entrance fee she cannot bring herself to collect, because the people she wants in the beds are exactly the people who have nothing. In 1903 she deeds the whole property to the AME Zion Church, which has the institutional weight she does not. In June of 1908 it opens.
suggested_refs: The Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged, 180 South Street, Auburn, New York

stops.name: Auburn, dying in the house she built for other people
stops.date_confidence: attested. Her age at death cannot be stated: the competing birth years of 1815, 1820, 1822, and 1825 put her anywhere between eighty-eight and ninety-eight.
stops.campa: She has been a resident of her own Home for two years by the time the pneumonia settles in, living in the building she raised for people who had nowhere. Family, friends, and church members are in the room. Her age cannot be given, then or now, because no one wrote down the day she was born and the estate that owned her kept no register of it. The wire services carry her death across the country within a day. The obituaries call her Moses, the working name from the years when saying her own would have got somebody hanged.
suggested_refs: Thompson Memorial AME Zion Church, Auburn, where her funeral was held

stops.name: Fort Hill Cemetery, buried with military honors
stops.date_confidence: attested to within days of the death; NPS confirms burial with military honors at Fort Hill without fixing the day. The replacement grave marker installed by the Empire State Federation of Women's Clubs in 1937 is [R], asserted in the dossier and not confirmed by any page reached.
stops.campa: They bury her at Fort Hill with military honors, a rifle salute over a woman the army never enlisted, never commissioned, and never paid at a scout's rate. The following year the city sets up a memorial tablet repeating Bradford's figures, nineteen trips and three hundred people brought out, so that a number written in 1868 to move copies of a pamphlet is now cut into stone. The archival count made a century later is smaller and much harder: about thirteen missions, about seventy people, by hand, at night, a few at a time.
suggested_refs: Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004), which reconstructs the mission count from estate records, advertisements, and the Still papers
Milton Sernett, Harriet Tubman: Myth, Memory, and History (2007)
sources: Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)
